claim: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) enhances voluntary motor output in humans with central nervous system damage.
source: Acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH) enhances voluntary motor output in humans with central nervous system damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established finding that motivates the current study.

claim: The amplitude of cortically and subcortically elicited MEPs increased for 75 min after AIH but not sham AIH.
source: We found that the amplitude of cortically and subcortically elicited MEPs increased for 75 min after AIH but not sham AIH while intracortical activity remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Intracortical activity remained unchanged after AIH.
source: We found that the amplitude of cortically and subcortically elicited MEPs increased for 75 min after AIH but not sham AIH while intracortical activity remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by SICI and ICF measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: AIH increased STDP outcomes.
source: Notably, AIH increased STDP outcomes while spinal motoneuron excitability remained unchanged.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Spinal motoneuron excitability remained unchanged after AIH.
source: Notably, AIH increased STDP outcomes while spinal motoneuron excitability remained unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by F-wave measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: AIH changes corticospinal function in humans by altering corticospinal-motoneuronal synaptic transmission.
source: Our results provide the first evidence that AIH changes corticospinal function in humans, likely by altering corticospinal-motoneuronal synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: AIH may represent a novel noninvasive approach for inducing spinal plasticity in humans.
source: AIH may represent a novel noninvasive approach for inducing spinal plasticity in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: AIH impacts the respiratory, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, bone and nervous systems.
source: Brief exposures to hypoxic air interspersed with periods of breathing ambient room air, known as acute intermittent hypoxia (AIH), impacts the respiratory, cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, bone and nervous systems (Dale et al., 2014; Gonzalez-Rothi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AIH triggers recovery of motor function in humans with partial paralysis due to spinal cord injury.
source: During recent years, an increasing number of studies support the view that AIH also affects the damaged central nervous system, triggering recovery of motor function in humans with partial paralysis due to spinal cord injury (Trumbower et al., 2012; Lynch et al., 2017; Navarrete-Opazo et al., 2017a, b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AIH represents a promising and safe strategy to supplement conventional neurorehabilitation.
source: AIH represents a promising and safe strategy to supplement conventional neurorehabilitation (Navarrete-Opazo and Mitchell, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Single and multiple exposures to AIH cause phrenic motor facilitation in animal models.
source: Studies in animal models have demonstrated that single and multiple exposures to AIH cause phrenic motor facilitation (Baker and Mitchell, 2000; Golder and Mitchell, 2005) and increase expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in respiratory motor neurons (Baker-Herman et al., 2004; Satriotomo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: AIH increases expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in respiratory motor neurons in animal models.
source: Studies in animal models have demonstrated that single and multiple exposures to AIH cause phrenic motor facilitation (Baker and Mitchell, 2000; Golder and Mitchell, 2005) and increase expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) in respiratory motor neurons (Baker-Herman et al., 2004; Satriotomo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Changes in the respiratory system after AIH are reflected as serotonin-dependent synaptic plasticity in the spinal cord.
source: Changes in the respiratory system are reflected as serotonin-dependent synaptic plasticity in the spinal cord (Bach and Mitchell, 1996; Fuller et al., 2001; Baker-Herman and Mitchell, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Exposure to AIH transiently increases sympathetic nerve activity.
source: For example, exposure to AIH transiently increases sympathetic nerve activity (Dick et al., 2007; Xing and Pilowsky, 2010) and connectivity of spinal interneurons projecting to midthoracic motoneurons (Streeter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AIH increases connectivity of spinal interneurons projecting to midthoracic motoneurons.
source: For example, exposure to AIH transiently increases sympathetic nerve activity (Dick et al., 2007; Xing and Pilowsky, 2010) and connectivity of spinal interneurons projecting to midthoracic motoneurons (Streeter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The corticospinal tract is a major descending motor pathway contributing to the control of voluntary movement.
source: The corticospinal tract is a major descending motor pathway contributing to the control of voluntary movement (Lemon, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Plasticity in the corticospinal tract contributes to the recovery of motor function in individuals with a variety of motor disorders.
source: Plasticity in the corticospinal tract contributes to the recovery of motor function in individuals with a variety of motor disorders (Ridding and Rothwell, 2007; Oudega and Perez, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Serotonin contributes to plasticity in the corticospinal pathway.
source: Serotonin (Batsikadze et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2016) and BDNF (Fritsch et al., 2010), which are both affected by AIH, contribute to plasticity in the corticospinal pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BDNF contributes to plasticity in the corticospinal pathway.
source: Serotonin (Batsikadze et al., 2013; Kuo et al., 2016) and BDNF (Fritsch et al., 2010), which are both affected by AIH, contribute to plasticity in the corticospinal pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Repetitive AIH enhances BDNF immunoreactivity in primary motor cortex of rats, especially around pyramidal cells of layer V.
source: Further, repetitive AIH enhances BDNF immunoreactivity in primary motor cortex of rats, especially around pyramidal cells of layer V (Satriotomo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Corticospinal transmission depends on the strength of synaptic connections between corticospinal drive and spinal motoneurons.
source: Since corticospinal transmission depends on the strength of synaptic connections between corticospinal drive and spinal motoneurons (Taylor and Martin, 2009; Bunday and Perez, 2012) and AIH induces spinal cord plasticity (Dale et al., 2014) we predicted that changes in spinal synapses contribute to AIH-mediated effects in corticospinal transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AIH induces spinal cord plasticity.
source: Since corticospinal transmission depends on the strength of synaptic connections between corticospinal drive and spinal motoneurons (Taylor and Martin, 2009; Bunday and Perez, 2012) and AIH induces spinal cord plasticity (Dale et al., 2014) we predicted that changes in spinal synapses contribute to AIH-mediated effects in corticospinal transmission.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after 15 min (29.4 ± 26.2%) following AIH compared with baseline.
source: Tukey Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (29.4 ± 26.2%; p<0.001), 30 (37.4 ± 23.2%; p<0.001), 45 (36.5 ± 38.3%; p<0.001), 60 (42.1 ± 20.0%; p<0.001) and 75 (36.0 ± 25.8%; p<0.001) min after AIH compared with baseline (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after 30 min (37.4 ± 23.2%) following AIH compared with baseline.
source: Tukey Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (29.4 ± 26.2%; p<0.001), 30 (37.4 ± 23.2%; p<0.001), 45 (36.5 ± 38.3%; p<0.001), 60 (42.1 ± 20.0%; p<0.001) and 75 (36.0 ± 25.8%; p<0.001) min after AIH compared with baseline (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after 45 min (36.5 ± 38.3%) following AIH compared with baseline.
source: Tukey Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (29.4 ± 26.2%; p<0.001), 30 (37.4 ± 23.2%; p<0.001), 45 (36.5 ± 38.3%; p<0.001), 60 (42.1 ± 20.0%; p<0.001) and 75 (36.0 ± 25.8%; p<0.001) min after AIH compared with baseline (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after 60 min (42.1 ± 20.0%) following AIH compared with baseline.
source: Tukey Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (29.4 ± 26.2%; p<0.001), 30 (37.4 ± 23.2%; p<0.001), 45 (36.5 ± 38.3%; p<0.001), 60 (42.1 ± 20.0%; p<0.001) and 75 (36.0 ± 25.8%; p<0.001) min after AIH compared with baseline (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after 75 min (36.0 ± 25.8%) following AIH compared with baseline.
source: Tukey Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (29.4 ± 26.2%; p<0.001), 30 (37.4 ± 23.2%; p<0.001), 45 (36.5 ± 38.3%; p<0.001), 60 (42.1 ± 20.0%; p<0.001) and 75 (36.0 ± 25.8%; p<0.001) min after AIH compared with baseline (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No changes were observed in MEP amplitude after the sham AIH protocol compared with baseline at any of the time points tested.
source: No changes were observed in MEP amplitude after the sham AIH protocol compared with baseline at any of the time point tested (all p=0.10).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the control condition.

claim: MEPs were facilitated in all subjects (19/19) after the AIH protocol when comparing baseline to the average of measurements between 15 and 75 min after AIH.
source: Note that MEPs were facilitated in all of subjects after the AIH protocol (19/19) when comparing baseline to the average of measurements between 15 and 75 min after AIH.
evidence: This describes the consistency of the effect across all participants.

claim: The MEP amplitude returned to baseline ~120 min after AIH in one individual.
source: We followed up the effects of AIH in one individual and found out that the MEP amplitude returned to baseline ~120 min after AIH.
evidence: This is a follow-up observation in a single subject.

claim: The magnitude of SICI remained similar to baseline immediately after, 30 min, and 60 min after the AIH protocol.
source: We found that the magnitude of SICI remained similar to baseline (37.9 ± 3.0%) immediately after (37.6 ± 4.5%), 30 (41.5 ± 5.3%) and 60 min (39.4 ± 6.9%) after the AIH protocol (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a negative finding showing no change in SICI after AIH.

claim: The magnitude of ICF remained similar to baseline immediately after, 30 min, and 60 min after the AIH protocol.
source: The magnitude of ICF remained similar to baseline (53.5 ± 25.3%) immediately after (62.1 ± 24.9%), 30 (62.0 ± 33.5%) and 60 min (62.1 ± 25.2%) after the AIH protocol (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a negative finding showing no change in ICF after AIH.

claim: MEP amplitude elicited by electrical stimulation increased after 15 min (1.16 ± 0.9 mV) following AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV).
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (1.16 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.01), 30 (1.18 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.007), 45 (1.19 ± 0.8 mV; p<0.001), 60 (1. 43 ± 1.1 mV; p<0.001), and 75 (1.15 ± 0.9; p=0.006) min after AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MEP amplitude elicited by electrical stimulation increased after 30 min (1.18 ± 0.9 mV) following AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV).
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (1.16 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.01), 30 (1.18 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.007), 45 (1.19 ± 0.8 mV; p<0.001), 60 (1. 43 ± 1.1 mV; p<0.001), and 75 (1.15 ± 0.9; p=0.006) min after AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MEP amplitude elicited by electrical stimulation increased after 45 min (1.19 ± 0.8 mV) following AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV).
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (1.16 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.01), 30 (1.18 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.007), 45 (1.19 ± 0.8 mV; p<0.001), 60 (1. 43 ± 1.1 mV; p<0.001), and 75 (1.15 ± 0.9; p=0.006) min after AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MEP amplitude elicited by electrical stimulation increased after 60 min (1.43 ± 1.1 mV) following AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV).
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (1.16 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.01), 30 (1.18 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.007), 45 (1.19 ± 0.8 mV; p<0.001), 60 (1. 43 ± 1.1 mV; p<0.001), and 75 (1.15 ± 0.9; p=0.006) min after AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: MEP amplitude elicited by electrical stimulation increased after 75 min (1.15 ± 0.9 mV) following AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV).
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased after 15 (1.16 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.01), 30 (1.18 ± 0.9 mV; p=0.007), 45 (1.19 ± 0.8 mV; p<0.001), 60 (1. 43 ± 1.1 mV; p<0.001), and 75 (1.15 ± 0.9; p=0.006) min after AIH compared with baseline (0.73 ± 0.4 mV; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the experimental results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No changes were observed in MEPs elicited by electrical stimulation immediately after the AIH protocol.
source: As for MEPs evoked by TMS, we observed no changes in MEPs elicited by electrical stimulation immediately after the AIH protocol (p=0.37).
evidence: This is a negative finding at the immediate post-AIH timepoint.

claim: MEPs elicited by electrical stimulation were facilitated in all subjects after the AIH protocol when comparing the average of tests conducted between 15 and 75 min after AIH with the baseline.
source: Note that MEPs were facilitated in all subjects after the AIH protocol when comparing the average of tests conducted between 15 and 75 min after AIH with the baseline.
evidence: This describes the consistency of the effect across all participants for electrically evoked MEPs.

claim: The M-max remained similar before and after AIH.
source: Note that the M-max remained similar before and after AIH (baseline = 17.4 ± 3.6 mV, after = 17.8 ± 3.6; p=0.2) and sham AIH (baseline = 17.7 ± 3.5 mV, after = 17.9 ± 3.5 mV; p=0.3).
evidence: This is a negative finding showing no change in M-max after AIH.

claim: F-wave amplitude remained similar to baseline across all time points after the AIH protocol.
source: The amplitude remained similar to baseline across time (baseline = 0.43 ± 0.4% of M-max; immediately after = 0.4 ± 0.3% of M-max; 15 min = 0.43 ± 0.4% of M-max; 30 min = 0. 46 ± 0.4% of M-max; 45 min = 0.44 ± 0.4% of M-max; 60 min = 0.41 ± 0.3% of M-max; 75 min = 0.43 ± 0.4% of M-max) after the AIH protocol.
evidence: This is a negative finding showing no change in F-wave amplitude after AIH.

claim: F-wave persistence remained similar to baseline across all time points after the AIH protocol.
source: The F-wave persistence remained similar to baseline across time (baseline = 62.2 ± 25.8%; immediately after = 59.5 ± 28.9%, 15 min = 58.6 ± 28.5%, 30 min = 62.8 ± 25.5%, 45 min = 63.1 ± 27.3%, 60 min = 62.4 ± 22.7%; 75 min = 59.4 ± 26.1%) after the AIH protocol.
evidence: This is a negative finding showing no change in F-wave persistence after AIH.

claim: MEP amplitude increased to a larger extent after STDPAIH (77.2 ± 63.5%) compared with STDPsham AIH (36.72 ± 31.1%) between 30 and 45 min after the protocol.
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased to a larger extent after STDPAIH (77.2 ± 63.5%) compared with STDPsham AIH (36.72 ± 31.1%, p=0.005) and AIH (24.78 ± 31.1%, p=0.007) between 30 and 45 min after the protocol.
evidence: This is a specific data point from the STDP experiment shown in Figure 6.

claim: MEP amplitude increased to a larger extent after STDPAIH (77.2 ± 63.5%) compared with AIH (24.78 ± 31.1%) between 30 and 45 min after the protocol.
source: Post hoc tests showed that MEP amplitude increased to a larger extent after STDPAIH (77.2 ± 63.5%) compared with STDPsham AIH (36.72 ± 31.1%, p=0.005) and AIH (24.78 ± 31.1%, p=0.007) between 30 and 45 min after the protocol.
evidence: This is a specific data point from the STDP experiment shown in Figure 6.

claim: MEPs were larger between 60 and 75 min after the STDPAIH (78.6 ± 52.1%) compared with STDPsham AIH (23.8 ± 31.7%).
source: Similarly, MEPs were larger between 60 and 75 min after the STDPAIH (78.6 ± 52.1%) compared with STDPsham AIH (23.8 ± 31.7%; p<0.001) and AIH protocol (38.1 ± 17.6%; p=0.009; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the STDP experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MEPs were larger between 60 and 75 min after the STDPAIH (78.6 ± 52.1%) compared with AIH protocol (38.1 ± 17.6%).
source: Similarly, MEPs were larger between 60 and 75 min after the STDPAIH (78.6 ± 52.1%) compared with STDPsham AIH (23.8 ± 31.7%; p<0.001) and AIH protocol (38.1 ± 17.6%; p=0.009; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a specific data point from the STDP experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MEP amplitude increased to a similar extent after STDPsham AIH and AIH immediately after, 30–45 min, and 60–75 min.
source: Note that MEP amplitude increased to a similar extent after STDPsham AIH and AIH immediately after (p=0.54), 30–45 min (p=0.99) and 60–75 min (p=0.17).
evidence: This is a comparison showing no significant difference between STDPsham AIH and AIH alone.

claim: MEP amplitude increased after STDPAIH (77.9 ± 53.1%) to a larger extent than the sum of the changes observed after STDPsham AIH and AIH (64.1 ± 32.2%) in most (8/11) participants.
source: Note that MEP amplitude increased after STDPAIH (77.9 ± 53.1%) to larger extent than the sum of the changes observed after STDPsham AIH and AIH (64.1 ± 32.2%) in most (8/11) participants.
evidence: This describes a synergistic effect in the majority of participants.

claim: The increases in MEP amplitude after STDPAIH correlated with increases in MEP amplitude after STDPsham AIH (r = 0.6, p=0.03).
source: Also note, that the increases in MEP amplitude after STDPAIH correlated with increases in MEP amplitude after STDPsham AIH (r = 0.6, p=0.03; Figure 6F) but not after AIH (r = 0.2, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The increases in MEP amplitude after STDPAIH did not correlate with increases after AIH (r = 0.2, p=0.4).
source: Also note, that the increases in MEP amplitude after STDPAIH correlated with increases in MEP amplitude after STDPsham AIH (r = 0.6, p=0.03; Figure 6F) but not after AIH (r = 0.2, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a negative correlation finding.

claim: Different factors increase the excitability of corticospinal neurons in humans including exercise, motor learning, repetitive stimulation of a peripheral nerve and/or cortical regions, and deafferentation.
source: Different factors increase the excitability of corticospinal neurons in humans including exercise, motor learning, repetitive stimulation of a peripheral nerve and/or cortical regions, and deafferentation (Brasil-Neto et al., 1993; Tazoe and Perez, 2015; Chung et al., 2016; Berghuis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Repeated AIH exposure in rats changes the neurochemical phenotype of corticospinal cells in ways that suggest enhanced function.
source: This agrees with evidence showing that repeated AIH exposure in rats changes the neurochemical phenotype of corticospinal cells in ways that suggest enhanced function (Satriotomo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: MEPs elicited by TMS likely reflect activation of corticospinal cells making direct and indirect (i.e. via interneurons) connections with spinal motoneurons.
source: MEPs elicited by TMS, used to measure corticospinal excitability, likely reflect activation of corticospinal cells making direct and indirect (i.e. via interneurons), connections with spinal motoneurons (Petersen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Exposure to sustained hypoxia for a similar amount of time as used in this study does not change corticospinal excitability.
source: In contrast, exposure to sustained hypoxia for a similar amount of time as used in our study does not change corticospinal excitability (Szubski et al., 2006; Goodall et al., 2010; Rupp et al., 2012), highlighting that the duration (chronic versus acute) and pattern (intermittent versus sustained) are of importance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SICI likely reflects activation of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) inhibitory circuits (GABAA) in the primary motor cortex.
source: Studies using pharmacology and epidural recordings indicate that SICI likely reflects activation of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) inhibitory circuits (GABAA) in the primary motor cortex (Hanajima et al., 1998; Di Lazzaro et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of changes in SICI after the AIH protocol suggests that it is less likely that changes in the primary motor cortex contributed to the results.
source: Therefore, the lack of changes in SICI after the AIH protocol suggests that it is less likely that changes in the primary motor cortex contributed to our results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SICI data.

claim: ICF is sensitive to changes in both GABAergic and glutamatergic transmission in the primary motor cortex.
source: ICF is sensitive to changes in both GABAergic (Ziemann et al., 1996a, b) and glutamatergic transmission (Liepert et al., 1997) in the primary motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of changes in ICF after AIH supports a non-cortical site of plasticity.
source: Similarly, the lack of changes in ICF after AIH support a non-cortical site of plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ICF data.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the primary motor cortex likely activates axons of pyramidal tract neurons in the subcortical white matter at the axon initial segment.
source: Electrical stimulation of the primary motor cortex likely activates axons of pyramidal tract neurons in the subcortical white matter at the axon initial segment (Day et al., 1989) whereas electrical stimulation of the cervicomedullary junction activates corticospinal axons directly and faraway from the cortex (Taylor and Gandevia, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the cervicomedullary junction activates corticospinal axons directly and faraway from the cortex.
source: Electrical stimulation of the primary motor cortex likely activates axons of pyramidal tract neurons in the subcortical white matter at the axon initial segment (Day et al., 1989) whereas electrical stimulation of the cervicomedullary junction activates corticospinal axons directly and faraway from the cortex (Taylor and Gandevia, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Changes in MEPs evoked by electrical stimulation after AIH have a subcortical origin.
source: Thus, a possible interpretation of our results is that changes in MEPs evoked by electrical stimulation after AIH have a subcortical origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrical stimulation data.

claim: The parallel time course of changes in the amplitude of MEPs elicited by both TMS and electrical stimulation after AIH supports a subcortical origin.
source: This is supported by the parallel time course of changes in the amplitude of MEPs elicited by both TMS and electrical stimulation after AIH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal pattern of the data.

claim: Even a single AIH exposure changes the connectivity of spinal interneurons that may project to relevant motoneurons in rats.
source: Further supporting this idea, rat studies demonstrate that even a single AIH exposure changes the connectivity of spinal interneurons that may project to relevant motoneurons (Streeter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Combined STDP and AIH caused larger increases in corticospinal excitability versus AIH alone or STDP combined with sham AIH.
source: Here, we found that combined STDP and AIH caused larger increases in corticospinal excitability versus AIH alone or STDP combined with sham AIH.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the STDP experiment.

claim: The facilitatory effect of AIH and STDP was larger than the sum of the changes caused by each protocol alone in the majority of participants, suggesting that these forms of plasticity share some overlapping mechanisms.
source: The facilitatory effect of AIH and STDP was larger than the sum of the changes caused by each protocol alone in the majority if participants, suggesting that these forms of plasticity share some overlapping mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the synergistic effect observed.

claim: STDP is thought to engage long-term potentiation (LTP)-like mechanisms that depend on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA).
source: STDP is thought to engage long-term potentiation (LTP)-like mechanisms that depend on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) (Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: AIH-induced phrenic motor facilitation requires NMDA receptor activation to maintain (versus initiate) plasticity.
source: AIH-induced phrenic motor facilitation requires NMDA receptor activation to maintain (versus initiate) plasticity (Fuller et al., 2000; McGuire et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: STDP-like changes elicited through repeated noninvasive stimulation is blocked by dextromethorphan, a drug that antagonizes NMDA receptors, in humans.
source: In humans, STDP-like changes elicited through repeated noninvasive stimulation is blocked by dextromethorphan, a drug that antagonizes NMDA receptors (Dongés et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Corticospinal responses returned to baseline ~120 hr after a single AIH session in one participant.
source: Note that in our study, we followed up the effect of AIH on corticospinal excitability in one participant and found that corticospinal responses returned to baseline ~120 hr after a single AIH session, consistent with previous results on ankle strength in people with spinal cord injury (Trumbower et al., 2012) and AIH-induced long-term facilitation of phrenic nerve activity in rats (Bach and Mitchell, 1996; Nichols et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a follow-up observation in a single subject, consistent with previous findings.

claim: Measurements of intracortical excitability after AIH, such as SICI and ICF, reflect NMDA receptor dependent mechanisms operating at the cortical level.
source: Measurements of intracortical excitability after AIH, such as SICI and ICF, also reflect NMDA receptor dependent mechanisms operating at the cortical level (Ziemann et al., 1998; Schwenkreis et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of change in SICI and ICF highlights the specificity of STDP and AIH at the spinal level.
source: Thus, the lack of change in these outcomes highlights the specificity of STPD and AIH at the spinal level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative findings for cortical measures.

claim: F-waves are an indirect measure of motoneuronal excitability.
source: An unexpected result was the lack of changes in the amplitude and persistence of F-waves after AIH because it is an indirect measure of motoneuronal excitability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about F-waves.

claim: Some limitations have been described in the extent to which F-waves measure motoneuron excitability.
source: Although some limitations have been described in the extent to which F-waves measure motoneuron excitability (Hultborn and Nielsen, 1995; Espiritu et al., 2003), this outcome measure is adequately sensitive to detect changes in motoneuron excitability in some experimental paradigms (Giesebrecht et al., 2011; Khan et al., 2012; Rossi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: F-waves are adequately sensitive to detect changes in motoneuron excitability in some experimental paradigms.
source: Although some limitations have been described in the extent to which F-waves measure motoneuron excitability (Hultborn and Nielsen, 1995; Espiritu et al., 2003), this outcome measure is adequately sensitive to detect changes in motoneuron excitability in some experimental paradigms (Giesebrecht et al., 2011; Khan et al., 2012; Rossi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Episodic release of serotonin from raphe spinal projections to the cervical spinal cord is necessary and sufficient for induction but not maintenance of AIH-induced long-term facilitation in phrenic motoneurons.
